title: Ch. 1 - Storage Engines Intro & Overview
description: OLTP vs. OLAP, storage engine tradeoffs, DBMS architecture, and row vs. column layouts.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an OLTP workload?
options: Large batch analytical queries over historical data
Short-lived read/write transactions on recent data
Periodic full-table aggregations for reporting
Write-once, read-many archival operations
questions.explanation: OLTP workloads are dominated by short-lived transactions that read and write small amounts of recent data, unlike OLAP workloads which focus on longer analytical queries.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of disk-based storage engines over in-memory storage engines?
options: Faster read latency for random access
Lower cost per unit of storage capacity
Simpler concurrency control mechanisms
Better performance for write-heavy workloads
questions.explanation: Disk-based systems are much cheaper per unit of storage than RAM, which is why they remain attractive for large durable datasets even though memory is faster.

questions.question: Which DBMS component is primarily responsible for choosing an efficient execution strategy for a query?
options: Transport system
Query optimizer
Recovery manager
Buffer manager
questions.explanation: The query optimizer evaluates alternative execution strategies and selects a plan. The execution engine then carries out that chosen plan.

questions.question: Which workload benefits most from a column-oriented layout?
options: Point lookups and small transactional updates across entire rows
Analytical scans that aggregate a few columns over many rows
Workloads that require every row to be stored contiguously for writes
Index maintenance on a single primary key
questions.explanation: Column stores are especially strong for analytical workloads because they can scan only the referenced columns instead of reading full rows.

questions.question: Which three high-level decisions describe many storage structure tradeoffs? (Select all that apply)
options: Buffering
Immutability
Ordering
Compression
questions.explanation: The notes frame many storage designs in terms of buffering, immutability, and ordering. Compression matters too, but it is not one of that core three-way framing decisions.

questions.question: What characterizes an HTAP system?
options: It only supports OLAP queries on archived data
It handles both transactional and analytical workloads in a unified engine
It replaces the storage engine with a pure in-memory cache
It requires separate physical clusters for reads and writes
questions.explanation: HTAP systems combine OLTP and OLAP capabilities so that analytical queries can run alongside transactional workloads without requiring a separate data warehouse.

questions.question: Which storage engine sub-components are typically found in a DBMS? (Select all that apply)
options: Transaction manager
Buffer manager
Recovery manager
Query parser
questions.explanation: The storage engine typically includes a transaction manager, lock manager, buffer manager, access methods, and recovery manager. The query parser belongs to the query processor layer above the storage engine.

questions.question: How do index-organized tables differ from heap-organized tables?
options: Index-organized tables store records in key order, while heap tables append records without ordering
Heap tables always require less disk space than index-organized tables
Index-organized tables cannot support range scans
Heap tables store records sorted by insertion timestamp
questions.explanation: Index-organized tables store records directly in the index structure in key order, making range scans efficient. Heap tables store records without any particular order, so they need separate index structures for efficient lookups.

questions.question: What is a key tradeoff when using a primary key as indirection for secondary indexes instead of storing direct file offsets?
options: Direct offsets are cheaper to update when the referenced record moves
Direct offsets always use less disk space
Primary key indirection eliminates the need for a primary index
Primary key indirection makes pointer updates cheaper but adds an extra lookup on reads
questions.explanation: When secondary indexes reference a primary key instead of a physical offset, moving a record only requires updating the primary index. The cost is an additional indirection step during reads.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of a row-oriented layout over a column-oriented layout?
options: It compresses individual columns more efficiently
It allows analytical scans to skip unused columns
It achieves better locality when accessing entire rows for transactional workloads
It reduces storage overhead for sparse data
questions.explanation: Row-oriented layouts store entire rows contiguously, which provides good spatial locality when a workload needs to read or write full rows, as is common in OLTP.

title: Ch. 2 - B-Tree Basics
description: B-Trees, B+Trees, balancing, fanout, and why databases prefer wide shallow trees.

questions.question: In a B-Tree, what happens when a leaf node becomes full and a new key must be inserted?
options: The tree is rebuilt from scratch
The key is stored in an overflow area
The node is split into two nodes and the median key is promoted to the parent
The oldest key in the node is evicted to make room
questions.explanation: When a node overflows, the tree splits it into two nodes and promotes a separator key upward. If the parent overflows too, the split can continue toward the root.

questions.question: Which properties are guaranteed by B-Trees? (Select all that apply)
options: All leaf nodes are at the same depth
Keys within each node are sorted
Each node contains exactly the same number of keys
The tree is always balanced
questions.explanation: B-Trees keep keys sorted and all leaves at the same depth, which makes them balanced. Nodes do not need to have exactly the same number of keys, only stay within occupancy bounds.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a B-Tree and a B+Tree?
options: B+Trees do not keep keys sorted within nodes
B-Trees store values in both internal and leaf nodes, while B+Trees store values only in leaf nodes
B+Trees cannot support range queries
B-Trees always have a higher branching factor than B+Trees
questions.explanation: In a B+Tree, internal nodes contain separator keys only, while actual values live in the leaves. That design increases fanout and makes range scans efficient.

questions.question: Why do database storage engines generally prefer wide, shallow trees over deep, narrow trees?
options: Deep trees use less memory overall
Fewer levels means fewer disk I/O operations to locate a key
Wide trees are easier to implement correctly
Narrow trees cannot store duplicate keys
questions.explanation: Every extra tree level can mean another page read. High fanout keeps the tree shallow, which reduces disk I/O for lookups.

questions.question: Why are plain binary search trees a poor fit for on-disk databases?
options: They cannot represent sorted data
They have low fanout and can require too many random seeks
They only support range queries
They must duplicate values in every internal node
questions.explanation: A binary search tree has fanout 2, which makes it tall. On disk, that means more random page reads and poor locality compared with wide trees like B-Trees.

questions.question: What usually happens when a B-Tree node underflows after deletions?
options: The entire tree is rebuilt immediately
The node is merged with or rebalanced against a sibling
The root is always deleted
The missing keys are reconstructed from the write-ahead log
questions.explanation: Underflow is commonly handled by merging with a sibling or redistributing keys. That fix can propagate upward if it changes parent occupancy.

questions.question: What does fanout refer to in the context of B-Trees?
options: The maximum number of children a node can have
The number of keys stored in each leaf node
The total number of nodes in the tree
The depth of the tree from root to any leaf
questions.explanation: Fanout is the maximum number of child pointers per node. Higher fanout creates wider, shallower trees that require fewer disk seeks for lookups.

questions.question: What is the role of separator keys in a B-Tree?
options: They encrypt the boundaries between subtrees
They divide the tree into subtrees with non-overlapping key ranges
They store pointers to overflow pages
They track which nodes have been recently accessed
questions.explanation: Separator keys (also called index entries or divider cells) define boundaries between subtrees. They are stored in sorted order within each internal node and guide lookups to the correct child.

questions.question: Why are sibling pointers useful in B+Trees?
options: They allow range queries to traverse leaves sequentially without revisiting parents
They eliminate the need for separator keys in internal nodes
They prevent node splits from ever occurring
They store backup copies of each key for crash recovery
questions.explanation: Sibling pointers link adjacent leaf nodes, enabling efficient range scans by following the chain of leaves instead of navigating back up and down the tree.

questions.question: Which statement about SSDs is correct regarding their internal write behavior?
options: SSDs can overwrite data in place at the byte level
SSDs erase individual pages independently without touching neighboring data
The smallest writable unit is a page, and pages can only be written to empty cells
The Flash Translation Layer is only used on HDDs
questions.explanation: SSDs write at page granularity and only to empty cells. Erasing happens at the larger block level. The Flash Translation Layer maps logical to physical page addresses and handles garbage collection.

title: Ch. 3 - File Formats
description: Slotted pages, binary encoding, endianness, page headers, and checksums for on-disk storage.

questions.question: What problem do slotted pages solve particularly well?
options: Encrypting records at rest
Managing variable-sized records inside a fixed-size page
Replicating pages across the network
Guaranteeing lock-free updates
questions.explanation: Slotted pages let a page hold variable-sized records while keeping stable indirection slots. That makes insertion, deletion, and defragmentation much easier.

questions.question: What does endianness describe in a binary file format?
options: Whether strings are null-terminated or length-prefixed
The byte order used to store multi-byte values
How page checksums are computed
Whether pages are compressed before writing
questions.explanation: Endianness refers to the byte order used for multi-byte numeric values, such as whether the most significant byte comes first or last.

questions.question: Why do databases store checksums or CRCs in page headers?
options: To choose a page replacement policy
To detect corruption when pages are read back
To make range scans faster
To avoid storing free space metadata
questions.explanation: Checksums and CRCs help detect corruption by verifying that the bytes read from disk still match what was written earlier.

questions.question: Which statements about slotted pages are true? (Select all that apply)
options: Pointers or slots can stay in sorted logical order even when cells move physically
They allow defragmentation without changing every external record reference
They require every record in a page to be exactly the same size
They commonly place metadata near the front of the page
questions.explanation: Slotted pages separate logical order from physical placement, which makes compaction practical. They are explicitly useful for variable-sized records, not fixed-size-only records.

questions.question: What is the difference between key cells and key-value cells in a B-Tree page?
options: Key cells store separator keys with child pointers, while key-value cells store keys with their associated data records
Key cells are used only in leaf nodes, while key-value cells are used in internal nodes
Key cells contain checksums, while key-value cells do not
There is no practical difference; the terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: Internal nodes use key cells that pair separator keys with child page pointers. Leaf nodes use key-value cells that pair keys with the actual stored records.

questions.question: How do slotted pages handle space freed by deleted records?
options: Freed space is immediately returned to the operating system
The entire page is rewritten after every deletion
Deleted cells are marked and their space is tracked in an availability list for reuse
Freed space is only reclaimed when the database is restarted
questions.explanation: When a cell is deleted, its space is added to an availability list (also called freeblocks). The page header tracks the first freeblock and total available bytes. If enough cumulative but non-contiguous space exists, defragmentation can consolidate it.

questions.question: Why must binary file formats in databases be versioned?
options: To allow the operating system to choose the right filesystem
To determine which compression algorithm to use at the hardware level
To encrypt data at rest using version-specific keys
To enable backward compatibility when the on-disk format evolves
questions.explanation: As database systems evolve, on-disk formats may change. Versioning ensures that older data files can still be read correctly, or that the system knows when a migration is needed.

title: Ch. 4 - Implementing B-Trees
description: Overflow pages, breadcrumbs, and bulk loading strategies in real-world B-Tree implementations.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of overflow pages in a B-Tree implementation?
options: To store replicas on remote machines
To extend a node when there is not enough contiguous space in its primary page
To replace sibling links during range scans
To guarantee that every node stays exactly half full
questions.explanation: Overflow pages let a logical node spill across multiple physical pages when the main page lacks enough space, especially with larger cells.

questions.question: What are breadcrumbs in B-Tree implementations?
options: A checksum stored in each child page
An in-memory stack of visited nodes used to propagate splits or merges upward
A linked list of all leaves in key order
A duplicate copy of the root page kept for crash recovery
questions.explanation: Breadcrumbs are the path remembered during traversal, often as an in-memory stack. They can be used instead of parent pointers when upward fixes are needed.

questions.question: Why is bulk loading efficient when the input is already sorted?
options: It prevents any future compaction
It lets the tree be built bottom-up with fewer splits and less random I/O
It eliminates the need for page headers
It guarantees all pages will remain perfectly full forever
questions.explanation: With sorted input, the tree can be built in large sequential chunks instead of repeatedly inserting and splitting nodes. That reduces maintenance work and random access during construction.

questions.question: What are magic numbers used for in B-Tree page headers?
options: To serve as constant multi-byte values for validation and sanity checks
To encrypt the page contents at rest
To store the page's position in the tree hierarchy
To record how many times a page has been accessed
questions.explanation: Magic numbers are fixed byte sequences placed in headers that help verify a page belongs to the expected format and has not been corrupted or misidentified.

questions.question: What is the advantage of rebalancing B-Tree nodes instead of immediately splitting or merging?
options: It guarantees every node is always exactly half full
It makes the tree immune to any further insertions or deletions
It eliminates the need for separator keys in parent nodes
It improves node occupancy and can reduce tree height by redistributing keys among siblings
questions.explanation: Rebalancing redistributes keys within a level to keep nodes more evenly filled, which can postpone or avoid splits and merges. The tradeoff is additional maintenance complexity.

questions.question: Why is the right-only append pattern efficient for auto-incrementing primary keys?
options: It distributes inserts evenly across all leaf nodes
It avoids the need for any B-Tree balancing operations
All new inserts go to the rightmost leaf, producing sequential writes with minimal fragmentation
It forces the tree to remain at exactly one level deep
questions.explanation: With monotonically increasing keys, inserts always land at the rightmost leaf. This produces sequential I/O and concentrates splits at the edge of the tree, reducing fragmentation. PostgreSQL calls this optimization fastpath.

questions.question: What happens to page identifiers freed during vacuum or maintenance operations?
options: They are immediately deallocated back to the operating system
They are added to a freelist so the space can be reused by future page allocations
They are converted into overflow pages automatically
They are permanently reserved and can never be reused
questions.explanation: Freed page IDs are added to a persistent freelist. This allows the database to reclaim and reuse that space for new pages without growing the file unnecessarily.

title: Ch. 5 - Transaction Processing and Recovery
description: ACID, write-ahead logging, ARIES, isolation anomalies, MVCC, locks, latches, and buffer management.

questions.question: Which properties are part of ACID? (Select all that apply)
options: Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Distribution
questions.explanation: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. Distribution is not one of the four guarantees.

questions.question: What is the core purpose of a write-ahead log (WAL)?
options: To compress pages before they reach disk
To record changes durably before the corresponding data pages are written
To keep all indexes perfectly balanced
To replace the buffer pool entirely
questions.explanation: A WAL ensures the log record describing a change reaches durable storage before the modified page does. That ordering is what enables crash recovery.

questions.question: Which buffer management policy combination is used by ARIES?
options: No-steal and force
Steal and no-force
No-steal and no-force
Steal and force
questions.explanation: ARIES assumes steal and no-force: pages may be flushed before commit, and committed transactions do not require forcing all updated pages immediately.

questions.question: Which anomaly can still happen under snapshot isolation?
options: Dirty read
Lost update
Write skew
Dirty write
questions.explanation: Snapshot isolation prevents many common anomalies, including dirty reads and many lost updates, but it still allows write skew because concurrent transactions can commit disjoint writes based on the same snapshot.

questions.question: What is the typical phase order in optimistic concurrency control (OCC)?
options: Write, read, validate
Read, validate, write
Validate, read, write
Read, write, rollback
questions.explanation: OCC usually lets a transaction read and buffer writes first, validates that its assumptions still hold, and only then applies writes.

questions.question: What is a major advantage of MVCC?
options: It guarantees no write amplification
It allows readers to observe older versions without blocking writers
It removes the need for transaction IDs
It stores only one version of every record
questions.explanation: MVCC keeps multiple versions of a record so readers can use a consistent snapshot while writers continue to create newer versions.

questions.question: What is the key difference between locks and latches?
options: Locks protect logical database contents, while latches protect physical in-memory structures
Locks are only used in distributed systems, while latches are only local
Locks are faster because they always avoid waiting
Latches provide serializable isolation, while locks do not
questions.explanation: Locks are about transaction-level correctness of database contents. Latches are short-term synchronization primitives that protect in-memory structures such as pages or tree nodes.

questions.question: How does the CLOCK page replacement algorithm approximate LRU?
options: By maintaining a perfect timestamp history for every page
By scanning pages in a circle and giving recently used pages a second chance
By evicting the most frequently used page first
By sorting all cached pages on every access
questions.explanation: CLOCK uses a circular structure and reference bits to cheaply approximate LRU. Pages that were used recently get another pass before eviction.

questions.question: What does a dirty page in the buffer pool represent?
options: A page modified in memory but not yet flushed to disk
A page that has been corrupted and needs repair
A page that has been evicted from the cache
A page currently locked by a background vacuum process
questions.explanation: A dirty page has been modified in the buffer pool but its changes have not yet been written back to durable storage. It must be flushed before it can be safely evicted.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Log Sequence Number (LSN) in write-ahead logging?
options: It assigns a unique, monotonically increasing identifier to each log record for ordering
It stores the physical disk address of each data page
It compresses log entries to reduce WAL file size
It determines which isolation level a transaction uses
questions.explanation: LSNs provide a total order on log records, ensuring they can be replayed in the correct sequence during recovery. Log records are flushed to disk in LSN order.

questions.question: Why do practical recovery systems often use physical logging for redo and logical logging for undo?
options: Physical redo is faster to replay, while logical undo handles concurrent modifications more gracefully
Logical redo is faster, but physical undo provides better crash safety
Physical logging is only possible for redo operations
There is no practical difference; the choice is arbitrary
questions.explanation: Physical redo records can be replayed quickly because they describe exact byte-level changes. Logical undo operations are more flexible when concurrent transactions have modified the same structures, since they describe the inverse operation rather than requiring a specific prior page state.

questions.question: Which isolation level allows dirty reads?
options: Read Committed
Repeatable Read
Read Uncommitted
Serializable
questions.explanation: Read Uncommitted is the weakest isolation level and allows a transaction to see changes from other transactions that have not yet committed, known as dirty reads.

questions.question: How are deadlocks typically detected in lock-based concurrency control?
options: By running a full table scan after every lock request
By timing out every transaction after a fixed global interval
By requiring all transactions to acquire locks in random order
By constructing a waits-for graph and checking it for cycles
questions.explanation: A waits-for graph tracks which transactions are waiting on locks held by other transactions. A cycle in this graph indicates a deadlock. Detection can run periodically or continuously.

questions.question: What is latch crabbing in the context of B-Tree concurrency?
options: Holding latches on every level of the tree simultaneously until the operation completes
Releasing parent latches early once it is clear the child operation will not require upward propagation
Replacing all latches with heavyweight transaction locks
Using copy-on-write to avoid latching entirely
questions.explanation: Latch crabbing is an optimistic technique where a traversal acquires a latch on the child and then releases the parent latch as soon as it determines the child is safe (will not split or merge). This reduces contention on upper tree levels.

title: Ch. 6 - B-Tree Variants
description: Copy-on-write trees, Bw-Trees, delta chains, and the tradeoffs B-Tree variants try to improve.

questions.question: What is a major tradeoff of copy-on-write B-Trees?
options: Readers must always block writers
They improve read isolation but can increase space and write costs
They cannot support snapshots
They require a log-structured merge tree underneath
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write trees avoid in-place modification, which helps readers and crash safety, but the extra copying increases write and space overhead.

questions.question: What is the role of delta chains in a Bw-Tree?
options: They store encrypted replicas for disaster recovery
They record incremental changes without rewriting the full node immediately
They replace quorums during consensus
They enforce strict page-level locking
questions.explanation: Bw-Trees append delta records that describe changes and chain them onto a logical node, delaying full consolidation until later.

questions.question: Which costs are B-Tree variants often trying to improve? (Select all that apply)
options: Write amplification
Space amplification
Latch contention
Network partition tolerance
questions.explanation: Many B-Tree variants are motivated by write cost, extra storage overhead, and synchronization complexity. Network partitions are a distributed systems concern, not a local index-structure goal.

questions.question: Why does LMDB not need a write-ahead log or compaction?
options: Its copy-on-write design writes new versions to new locations, keeping old versions intact until replaced
It stores all data exclusively in memory with no durability
It uses log-structured merge trees internally
It relies on the operating system's journaling filesystem for all crash safety
questions.explanation: LMDB uses copy-on-write B-Trees that never modify existing pages. It holds only two root versions (latest committed and pending), so old data is always readable and crash recovery is inherent in the structure.

questions.question: How does a Bw-Tree achieve lock-free operations?
options: By using heavyweight OS-level mutexes on each node
By requiring all writers to acquire a global latch before any modification
By installing new delta nodes into a mapping table via compare-and-swap (CAS)
By serializing all operations through a single coordinator thread
questions.explanation: The Bw-Tree uses an indirection mapping table where logical node identifiers map to physical locations. Updates install new delta nodes by atomically swapping pointers with CAS, avoiding traditional latches entirely.

questions.question: What is the core idea behind FD-Trees?
options: They use gossip protocols to disseminate index updates
They buffer updates in a small B-Tree and periodically merge them into larger immutable sorted runs with fractional cascading
They store all data in a single append-only log with no indexing
They replicate the B-Tree across multiple machines for fault tolerance
questions.explanation: FD-Trees absorb writes in a small mutable B-Tree buffer. When full, its contents are merged into immutable sorted runs of increasing size. Fractional cascading provides efficient cross-level search via bridge pointers between levels.

questions.question: What problem does the van Emde Boas layout solve for cache-oblivious B-Trees?
options: It guarantees zero write amplification
It encrypts tree nodes for secure storage
It eliminates the need for separator keys
It arranges subtrees in contiguous memory to maximize cache line utilization across different hardware
questions.explanation: The van Emde Boas layout recursively splits a tree at the middle level and stores each subtree contiguously in memory. This produces good cache behavior across different memory hierarchies without needing to know cache sizes at design time.

title: Ch. 7 - Log-Structured Storage
description: LSM Trees, tombstones, leveled compaction, Bloom filters, RUM, and SSTables.

questions.question: Which description best matches an LSM Tree?
options: A purely in-memory tree with no durability mechanism
A structure with a mutable in-memory memtable and immutable on-disk components
A tree that stores values only in internal nodes
A hash table that cannot support range queries
questions.explanation: An LSM Tree buffers writes in memory and periodically flushes sorted immutable structures to disk, reconciling them later with compaction.

questions.question: Why are tombstones used in LSM Trees?
options: To immediately remove a key from every on-disk table
To represent deletes without rewriting all older disk components immediately
To avoid storing keys in memtables
To guarantee zero read amplification
questions.explanation: Because disk components are immutable, a delete is usually recorded as a tombstone and reconciled later during reads and compaction.

questions.question: What is a defining trait of leveled compaction?
options: All tables at every level are allowed to overlap arbitrarily
Data is merged into levels with target sizes and controlled overlap
It never rewrites data after flushing
It keeps only one disk component at all times
questions.explanation: Leveled compaction organizes data into levels with size goals and carefully managed overlap, which usually improves reads at the cost of more rewrite work.

questions.question: Which statement about Bloom filters is correct?
options: They can produce false negatives but never false positives
They can produce false positives but never false negatives
They store exact key-value pairs in compressed form
They eliminate the need for SSTables
questions.explanation: Bloom filters are probabilistic membership structures: they may claim a key might exist when it does not, but they should not miss a key that was inserted.

questions.question: What does the RUM Conjecture say in practice?
options: Reducing read cost and update cost usually increases memory overhead
Any system can optimize reads, writes, and memory simultaneously
Read amplification is always worse than space amplification
Memory overhead matters only for in-memory databases
questions.explanation: The RUM framing says there is a tradeoff between read cost, update cost, and memory overhead. Pushing down two dimensions usually makes the third more expensive.

questions.question: What is a core property of an SSTable?
options: Keys are stored in random order to speed writes
It is a sorted on-disk table, typically paired with an index
It only works for fixed-size records
It requires every lookup to scan the full file
questions.explanation: Sorted String Tables store keys in sorted order on disk, often with an accompanying index to make lookups and range scans efficient.

questions.question: How does size-tiered compaction differ from leveled compaction?
options: Size-tiered compaction groups tables by size and merges similarly-sized tables, while leveled compaction maintains size-bounded levels with controlled overlap
Leveled compaction never rewrites data, while size-tiered compaction always does
Size-tiered compaction requires a write-ahead log, while leveled compaction does not
They are identical strategies with different names
questions.explanation: Size-tiered compaction merges tables of similar size into larger ones, risking temporary space spikes. Leveled compaction organizes data into levels with target sizes and merges across levels to control overlap, generally improving read performance at the cost of more write work.

questions.question: What is a merge-iteration in the context of LSM Trees?
options: A multi-way merge sort over sorted disk-resident tables, typically using a priority queue
A process that deletes all tombstones from the memtable
A single pass that rewrites the entire database into one file
An in-memory binary search across all SSTables simultaneously
questions.explanation: Merge-iteration performs a multi-way merge sort across multiple sorted on-disk tables using a priority queue or min-heap, producing a single sorted stream for reads or compaction output.

questions.question: Which amplification tradeoffs are inherent to LSM Trees? (Select all that apply)
options: Read amplification from consulting multiple tables for a single lookup
Write amplification from repeated rewrites during compaction
Space amplification from storing multiple versions of the same key
Network amplification from replicating compaction results to remote nodes
questions.explanation: LSM Trees face read amplification (checking multiple levels), write amplification (compaction rewrites), and space amplification (redundant key versions). Network amplification is a distributed systems concern, not inherent to the LSM Tree data structure itself.

questions.question: How does Bitcask differ from a traditional LSM Tree?
options: Bitcask stores keys sorted on disk, while LSM Trees do not
Bitcask does not support point queries
Bitcask uses leveled compaction, while LSM Trees use size-tiered
Bitcask appends records in insertion order without sorting and relies on an in-memory hash index for lookups
questions.explanation: Bitcask is an unordered log-structured engine. Records are appended directly to log files, and an in-memory keydir hash map provides O(1) point lookups. The tradeoff is that range queries are not efficiently supported.

questions.question: What problem does log stacking cause when multiple log-structured layers are combined?
options: It eliminates all write amplification
It improves read performance by caching at every layer
Redundant garbage collection and remapping across layers compound write amplification and fragmentation
It reduces the need for a Flash Translation Layer
questions.explanation: When an LSM Tree runs on top of a log-structured filesystem on top of an SSD with its own FTL, each layer independently performs garbage collection and remapping. This stacking produces compounded write amplification, fragmentation, and wasted work.

title: Ch. 8 - Distributed Systems Intro & Overview
description: Fallacies of distributed computing, perfect links, consensus limits, and failure models.

questions.question: Which statement is one of the fallacies of distributed computing?
options: The network is reliable
Local clocks can drift
Messages may be delayed
Partitions can happen
questions.explanation: One classic fallacy is assuming the network is reliable. Real distributed systems must expect delay, loss, partitions, and partial failure.

questions.question: Which delivery semantic allows duplicates but tries not to lose messages?
options: At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once processing
FIFO-only delivery
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery favors eventual delivery, which means duplicates are possible unless the receiver deduplicates or uses idempotent operations.

questions.question: Which properties belong to perfect links? (Select all that apply)
options: Reliable delivery
No duplication
No creation
Bounded latency
questions.explanation: Perfect links are defined in terms of correct delivery semantics: messages are delivered reliably, not duplicated, and not fabricated. They do not promise a fixed latency bound.

questions.question: What does the Two Generals Problem illustrate?
options: A leader can always be elected with enough retries
Agreement is impossible to guarantee with unreliable communication and no final confirmation
Checksums are insufficient for disk recovery
Clock synchronization is easy if both sides ping often
questions.explanation: The Two Generals Problem shows why common knowledge is hard to establish over unreliable asynchronous links: the final acknowledgment can always be uncertain.

questions.question: What does FLP impossibility say?
options: Consensus is impossible even in synchronous systems
Consensus cannot be guaranteed to terminate in a purely asynchronous system with even a single crash failure
Consensus always requires Byzantine fault tolerance
Consensus is only possible with three-phase commit
questions.explanation: FLP shows that in a purely asynchronous system, a deterministic consensus algorithm cannot guarantee termination if even one process may fail by crashing.

questions.question: Which failure model is the most severe among these?
options: Crash-stop
Crash-recovery
Omission fault
Byzantine fault
questions.explanation: Byzantine faults are the most adversarial because a node can behave arbitrarily, including lying, equivocating, or sending inconsistent messages.

questions.question: How does the crash-recovery failure model differ from crash-stop?
options: Crash-recovery assumes a crashed process never restarts
Crash-recovery only applies to network links, not processes
Crash-stop allows arbitrary message fabrication
In crash-recovery, a process may stop and later resume, requiring durable state for correctness
questions.explanation: Under crash-stop, a failed process is permanently gone. Crash-recovery allows processes to restart after a failure, but the algorithm must account for recovery using persisted state.

questions.question: Why is idempotency important in distributed systems?
options: It ensures that applying the same operation multiple times produces the same result as applying it once
It guarantees messages are delivered in FIFO order
It prevents all network partitions
It eliminates the need for acknowledgments
questions.explanation: In systems with at-least-once delivery, messages may be retried. Idempotent operations are safe to re-execute without causing unintended side effects, making retries harmless.

questions.question: What is the difference between a synchronous and an asynchronous distributed system model?
options: Synchronous systems have no failures, while asynchronous systems have only Byzantine failures
Asynchronous systems are always faster than synchronous systems
In a synchronous model, there are known bounds on message delivery and processing time; in an asynchronous model, there are no such bounds
Synchronous models do not allow message passing
questions.explanation: A synchronous system assumes bounded message delivery times and processing speeds, making timeouts reliable for failure detection. An asynchronous system makes no timing guarantees, which is why results like FLP impossibility apply.

questions.question: What strategies help prevent cascading failures in distributed systems? (Select all that apply)
options: Circuit breakers that stop forwarding requests to failing components
Exponential backoff with jitter to spread retry load
Increasing the retry rate as errors accumulate
Process-local queues to absorb short-time bursts
questions.explanation: Circuit breakers, backoff with jitter, and local queues all help contain failures. Increasing the retry rate under errors would worsen the problem by amplifying load on already-struggling components.

title: Ch. 9 - Failure Detection
description: Pings, heartbeats, Phi-Accrual detectors, and gossip-based failure detection.

questions.question: What is the difference between a ping and a heartbeat?
options: A ping is passive and a heartbeat is encrypted
A ping is request-response, while a heartbeat is an active signal sent to peers
A heartbeat always guarantees failure detection accuracy
A ping can only be used in synchronous systems
questions.explanation: A ping asks for a response within some time window, while a heartbeat is proactively emitted by a process to indicate it is still alive.

questions.question: What is the main idea behind a Phi-Accrual failure detector?
options: It declares every missing heartbeat an immediate crash
It outputs a continuous suspicion level instead of a strict up/down answer
It requires synchronized physical clocks across the cluster
It only works with centralized leaders
questions.explanation: Phi-Accrual models suspicion continuously based on heartbeat timing history, so downstream systems can choose their own threshold for acting on failures.

questions.question: How does gossip-based failure detection usually work?
options: A single leader polls every node in sequence
Nodes periodically exchange heartbeat counters or timestamps with random peers
Failures are inferred only from write-ahead logs
Each process must know the full network topology exactly
questions.explanation: Gossip protocols spread liveness information by having nodes periodically share state with random peers, which gradually gives the cluster a broad view of failures.

questions.question: What is the fundamental tradeoff in failure detector design?
options: Throughput versus durability
Consistency versus partition tolerance
Write amplification versus read amplification
Accuracy versus efficiency: detecting failures quickly risks more false positives
questions.explanation: Faster detection requires shorter timeouts or more aggressive monitoring, which increases the chance of falsely suspecting a healthy but slow process. More conservative settings reduce false positives but delay true failure detection.

questions.question: What does outsourced heartbeats add beyond direct heartbeat monitoring?
options: It replaces all heartbeats with synchronized physical clocks
It eliminates the need for any failure detection entirely
It uses information from a process's neighbors to detect failures even when direct communication is blocked
It guarantees zero false positives in all network conditions
questions.explanation: Outsourced heartbeats incorporate liveness information from neighboring processes, so a node can be considered reachable even if the direct link to the monitor is down. This accounts for both direct and indirect reachability.

title: Ch. 10 - Leader Election
description: Leader election, the Bully Algorithm, and why practical systems require majority agreement.

questions.question: In the Bully Algorithm, which process should ultimately become leader if all messages are delivered?
options: The process with the lowest rank
The process that initiated the election
The highest-ranked live process
Whichever process has the oldest local clock
questions.explanation: The Bully Algorithm relies on process ranking: the highest-ranked live process eventually suppresses lower-ranked candidates and becomes leader.

questions.question: Why do practical leader-based systems usually require a majority, not just any local election result?
options: To compress election messages
To prevent split brain during partitions
To eliminate the need for failure detection
To make clocks perfectly synchronized
questions.explanation: Without majority-based coordination, partitions can each believe they have a leader. Requiring a majority helps ensure only one side can proceed safely.

questions.question: What is split brain in the context of leader election?
options: A situation where a network partition causes multiple nodes to simultaneously believe they are the leader
A technique for distributing load evenly across all nodes
A method for splitting large B-Tree nodes during rebalancing
A consensus algorithm designed for Byzantine environments
questions.explanation: Split brain occurs when a network partition isolates groups of nodes that each independently elect their own leader. Both sides may accept writes, leading to divergent state that is difficult to reconcile.

questions.question: How does the Ring Algorithm for leader election work?
options: Each node broadcasts to all other nodes simultaneously
Nodes form a logical ring and pass a list of live nodes around it, electing the highest-ranked
The node with the lowest latency to a central coordinator is chosen
Nodes randomly select a leader using cryptographic coin flips
questions.explanation: In the Ring Algorithm, nodes are arranged in a circular doubly-linked list. A node that detects a leader failure contacts its next alive successor and passes along a set of live candidates. The highest-ranked node in the collected set becomes the new leader.

questions.question: What do the liveness and safety properties mean for leader election?
options: Liveness means the election eventually completes; safety means there is at most one leader at a time
Liveness means messages are encrypted; safety means nodes never crash
Liveness means all nodes agree on the same log; safety means writes are durable
Both properties are guarantees about network bandwidth
questions.explanation: Liveness guarantees that the system will eventually have a leader (the election terminates). Safety guarantees that at most one node acts as leader at any given time, preventing conflicting decisions.

title: Ch. 11 - Replication and Consistency
description: CAP, linearizability, consistency models, quorum reads and writes, CRDTs, and session guarantees.

questions.question: What does CAP say specifically during a network partition?
options: A system can simultaneously guarantee strict consistency and full availability
A system must choose between consistency and availability while tolerating the partition
Partition tolerance is optional in a distributed database
CAP only applies when nodes crash, not when links fail
questions.explanation: CAP is about tradeoffs under partition. If the network splits, a system cannot provide both strong consistency and full availability at the same time.

questions.question: Which consistency model is usually described as the strongest practical one?
options: Eventual consistency
Causal consistency
Linearizability
PRAM consistency
questions.explanation: Linearizability is often treated as the strongest practical consistency model because operations appear to take effect atomically at a single point in real time.

questions.question: Which statements about consistency models are true? (Select all that apply)
options: Sequential consistency requires all processes to observe the same operation order
Causal consistency preserves the order of causally related operations
Eventual consistency requires every read to return the latest value immediately
Strict consistency is stronger than linearizability
questions.explanation: Sequential consistency enforces one shared order, causal consistency preserves causal dependencies, and strict consistency is an even stronger idealized model than linearizability. Eventual consistency does not promise immediate latest reads.

questions.question: In tunable consistency, why is the condition R + W > N important?
options: It guarantees every read is lock-free
It ensures read and write quorums overlap on at least one replica
It prevents all network partitions
It eliminates the need for replication
questions.explanation: If read and write quorums overlap, a read is more likely to observe at least one replica that knows about the latest successful write.

questions.question: What is a defining goal of CRDTs?
options: They require centralized locking to merge safely
They are designed so replicas can merge divergent states into a valid converged result
They forbid replication entirely
They always provide linearizability
questions.explanation: CRDTs are built so that concurrent updates can be merged deterministically without conflicts, giving strong eventual consistency.

questions.question: Which session guarantee says a client should be able to see its own earlier writes?
options: Monotonic reads
Read-your-writes
Sequential consistency
Atomic broadcast
questions.explanation: Read-your-writes ensures a client session will not lose visibility of updates it already performed.

questions.question: What do the Harvest and Yield concepts offer beyond CAP?
options: They prove that partition tolerance is always optional
They replace linearizability with a weaker model
They provide tunable, quantitative measures of result completeness and request success rate
They eliminate the need for replication
questions.explanation: Harvest measures how complete a query result is (e.g., responses from 99 of 100 shards), and yield measures the fraction of requests that succeed. Together they let systems make nuanced tradeoffs rather than the binary consistency-or-availability choice of CAP.

questions.question: What is a linearization point?
options: The moment a transaction acquires its first lock
The final message in a two-phase commit protocol
The point where a B-Tree node splits into two children
The single instant between invocation and completion at which an operation appears to take effect atomically
questions.explanation: Under linearizability, every operation must appear to execute atomically at some point between its start and end. That point is the linearization point, and it defines the real-time ordering of operations.

questions.question: What are vector clocks used for in distributed systems?
options: Establishing a partial order of events and detecting causal relationships between operations
Synchronizing physical wall clocks across all nodes
Compressing replicated data for network efficiency
Encrypting messages between replicas
questions.explanation: Vector clocks let each process maintain a vector of logical timestamps. By comparing vectors, the system can determine whether two events are causally related or concurrent, enabling causal consistency implementations.

questions.question: What is the monotonic reads guarantee?
options: Every write from a session is applied before the next write begins
All clients always see the same value at the same time
Once a client reads a value, subsequent reads will never return an older value
Reads always return the value written by the most recent transaction globally
questions.explanation: Monotonic reads ensures that within a session, a client's view of the data never moves backward. If a read returns version N, future reads will return version N or newer.

questions.question: What is the purpose of witness replicas in tunable consistency?
options: They store the full dataset and serve all read requests
They perform compaction on behalf of other replicas
They replace the leader in consensus algorithms
They record that a write occurred without storing the full data, reducing storage cost while preserving quorum mechanics
questions.explanation: Witness replicas participate in quorum votes by recording write metadata without storing full copies of the data. They can be promoted to full replicas if needed, providing a cost-effective way to maintain quorum overlap.

title: Ch. 12 - Anti-Entropy & Dissemination
description: Read repair, hinted handoff, Merkle Trees, and anti-entropy mechanisms for convergence.

questions.question: What is read repair?
options: A background process that rewrites every SSTable nightly
A repair triggered by reads when replicas are compared and stale ones are updated
A way to compress replication logs
A lock manager optimization for hot rows
questions.explanation: Read repair detects divergence during a read and uses the fresh value to repair stale replicas, either synchronously or asynchronously.

questions.question: What problem does hinted handoff address?
options: Balancing B-Tree page occupancy
Temporarily unavailable replicas during writes
Consensus leader election
Checksum collisions in Merkle Trees
questions.explanation: Hinted handoff lets another node temporarily hold a write intended for an unavailable replica and forward it later when that replica recovers.

questions.question: Why are Merkle Trees useful for anti-entropy?
options: They avoid hashing entirely
They let replicas quickly narrow down which key ranges differ by comparing hashes hierarchically
They guarantee total order broadcast
They replace quorum reads
questions.explanation: Merkle Trees summarize data with hashes from leaves to root. Matching hashes let replicas skip equal ranges and focus only on divergent subtrees.

questions.question: What are sloppy quorums and what do they trade?
options: They allow writes to non-designated replicas when target nodes are unavailable, improving availability at the cost of consistency
They require strict majority agreement for every operation
They eliminate the need for any replication
They guarantee linearizable reads under all conditions
questions.explanation: Sloppy quorums relax the requirement that quorum members be the designated replicas. Combined with hinted handoff, this improves write availability during partial failures, but the consistency guarantee is weakened because the write may not reach the canonical replicas immediately.

questions.question: How do digest requests optimize read repair?
options: They skip reading from any replica entirely
Replicas return a hash of their data instead of the full value, and full reads are issued only when hashes disagree
They compress all replica responses into a single network packet
They force all replicas to return the same value regardless of their actual state
questions.explanation: Digest requests reduce network overhead during read repair. The coordinator asks replicas for a compact hash rather than the full data. Only when digests differ does the coordinator fetch full values to determine which replica is stale and needs updating.

questions.question: What distinguishes gossip dissemination from simple broadcasting?
options: Gossip sends messages to every node simultaneously in a single round
Gossip spreads information probabilistically through random peer exchanges, trading message redundancy for robustness
Gossip requires a centralized message broker
Broadcasting is probabilistic while gossip is deterministic
questions.explanation: Gossip protocols propagate information by having each node periodically share state with randomly selected peers. This epidemic-style spread is inherently redundant but highly robust against individual node or link failures, unlike broadcasting which is simpler but more fragile at scale.

title: Ch. 13 - Distributed Transactions
description: Two-phase commit, three-phase commit, consistent hashing, and contrasting Calvin with Spanner.

questions.question: What are the two phases of two-phase commit (2PC)?
options: Election and replication
Prepare and commit-or-abort
Read and repair
Snapshot and merge
questions.explanation: In 2PC, the coordinator first asks participants to prepare and vote, then announces a final commit or abort decision.

questions.question: Why is classic 2PC considered blocking?
options: Because it requires byzantine quorums
Because participants may have to wait indefinitely if the coordinator fails at the wrong time
Because it never writes anything to disk
Because it only works with deterministic schedulers
questions.explanation: If the coordinator fails after some participants have prepared but before they learn the final decision, they may be stuck waiting and unable to decide safely on their own.

questions.question: What problem is three-phase commit (3PC) trying to reduce compared with 2PC?
options: The cost of Merkle Tree construction
Blocking after coordinator failure
Read amplification in LSM Trees
The need for write-ahead logging
questions.explanation: 3PC adds an extra phase so participants spend less time in an ambiguous state, reducing some blocking scenarios compared with 2PC.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of consistent hashing over a naive hash(key) % N approach?
options: It guarantees perfect load balance for every workload
It reduces how much data must move when nodes are added or removed
It removes the need for replication
It forces all writes through a single coordinator
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing maps data onto a ring so node changes only affect nearby ranges, avoiding a near-global reshuffle of keys.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts Calvin and Spanner?
options: Calvin relies on deterministic ordering, while Spanner combines 2PC with Paxos groups and TrueTime
Calvin is leaderless, while Spanner uses only local clocks with no coordination
Spanner avoids multi-partition coordination entirely, while Calvin uses sloppy quorums
Both systems are described as unordered eventually consistent stores
questions.explanation: The notes present Calvin as deterministic and sequence-driven, while Spanner combines distributed transactions with Paxos-backed shards and its TrueTime API.

questions.question: What role does Spanner's TrueTime API serve?
options: It replaces the need for any consensus protocol
It eliminates all network latency between data centers
It provides high-precision wall-clock timestamps used for transaction ordering and consistency
It is a deterministic scheduler like Calvin's sequencer
questions.explanation: TrueTime exposes bounded clock uncertainty, allowing Spanner to assign globally meaningful timestamps to transactions. This enables consistent snapshot reads and ordering without requiring a single global sequencer.

questions.question: What is the Percolator model's approach to handling write conflicts under snapshot isolation?
options: It uses pessimistic locking to prevent any concurrent writes
It applies a first-commit-wins rule: conflicting writes are aborted and retried
It merges conflicting writes using CRDTs
It ignores conflicts entirely and relies on eventual consistency
questions.explanation: Percolator provides snapshot isolation using MVCC. When two transactions conflict on the same key, the first to commit wins and the other is aborted and must retry. This prevents lost updates but does not prevent write skew.

questions.question: What does coordination avoidance aim to achieve?
options: It forces all operations through a single coordinator for simplicity
It requires Byzantine fault tolerance for all operations
It eliminates replication to avoid coordination overhead
It identifies operations that can execute correctly without cross-node coordination, improving performance and scalability
questions.explanation: Coordination avoidance uses the concept of invariant confluence (I-confluence) to determine which operations can safely execute independently on different replicas and still produce a valid merged result, avoiding the latency and availability costs of coordination.

questions.question: How does database sharding relate to distributed transactions?
options: Sharding eliminates the need for distributed transactions entirely
Each shard is a single source for a data subset, so transactions spanning multiple shards require coordination protocols like 2PC
Sharding guarantees linearizability across all partitions by default
Shards always use consistent hashing, never range-based partitioning
questions.explanation: Sharding splits data across replica sets where each set owns a subset. Single-shard transactions are local and fast, but transactions that touch multiple shards require distributed commit protocols to maintain atomicity.

title: Ch. 14 - Consensus
description: Atomic broadcast, Paxos, Multi-Paxos, Raft, and Byzantine fault tolerance.

questions.question: What two properties distinguish atomic broadcast? (Select all that apply)
options: All-or-none delivery among correct processes
A single global delivery order
Guaranteed zero latency
Local-only message scope
questions.explanation: Atomic broadcast combines reliable delivery with total ordering, so correct processes deliver the same messages in the same order.

questions.question: Which roles appear in classic Paxos? (Select all that apply)
options: Proposers
Acceptors
Learners
Coordinated witnesses
questions.explanation: Classic Paxos is usually described in terms of proposers, acceptors, and learners. Witnesses are discussed elsewhere in replication, not as a core Paxos role.

questions.question: If a Paxos deployment wants to tolerate f failures, how many acceptors are typically needed and what size quorum is required?
options: f total, quorum 1
2f + 1 total, quorum f + 1
3f + 1 total, quorum 2f + 1
f + 1 total, quorum f
questions.explanation: Classic Paxos commonly uses 2f + 1 acceptors so that any quorum of f + 1 intersects with every other quorum.

questions.question: What is the main optimization of Multi-Paxos?
options: It removes quorums entirely
It reuses a stable leader so the expensive prepare phase does not need to run for every value
It allows arbitrary Byzantine behavior
It stores no log of chosen values
questions.explanation: Once a leader is established, Multi-Paxos can often skip repeating the full leader-establishment work for each new log entry.

questions.question: Which three roles are central in Raft?
options: Candidate, leader, follower
Primary, acceptor, learner
Coordinator, cohort, witness
Publisher, subscriber, relay
questions.explanation: Raft uses followers as the default role, candidates during elections, and a leader that handles replication and client interaction.

questions.question: How does Raft usually resolve split votes during an election?
options: By requiring synchronized physical clocks
By using randomized election timers and starting a new term if needed
By letting every partition keep its own permanent leader
By choosing the node with the most uncommitted entries automatically
questions.explanation: Raft uses randomized timeouts so competing candidates are less likely to keep colliding in repeated elections.

questions.question: How many replicas are needed to tolerate f Byzantine faults in PBFT?
questions.explanation: PBFT requires 3f + 1 replicas to tolerate up to f Byzantine failures while still collecting enough matching responses.

questions.question: What are the three phases of Zookeeper Atomic Broadcast (ZAB)?
options: Discovery, synchronization, broadcast
Propose, accept, learn
Pre-prepare, prepare, commit
Read, validate, write
questions.explanation: ZAB operates in three phases: Discovery (collecting latest transaction IDs and proposing a new epoch), Synchronization (ensuring followers share the same history), and Broadcast (the leader orders and distributes messages).

questions.question: What does a term (or epoch) represent in Raft?
options: A monotonically increasing logical time period that provides ordering without clock synchronization
A fixed wall-clock time interval measured in seconds
The number of log entries a leader has committed
The physical network latency between nodes
questions.explanation: Raft terms are monotonically increasing counters that establish a global partial ordering of events. Each term has at most one leader, and terms increase with each new election, providing a logical notion of time without requiring synchronized clocks.

questions.question: What is the key difference between best-effort broadcast and reliable broadcast?
options: Reliable broadcast is faster because it sends fewer messages
Best-effort broadcast guarantees total order while reliable broadcast does not
In best-effort broadcast, delivery fails if the sender crashes; reliable broadcast ensures all correct processes deliver the message even if the sender fails
They are identical in guarantees but differ in implementation language
questions.explanation: Best-effort broadcast depends on the sender remaining alive. If the sender crashes mid-broadcast, some processes may never receive the message. Reliable broadcast adds retransmission so all correct processes eventually deliver the message regardless of sender failure.

questions.question: How does Fast Paxos reduce latency compared with classic Paxos?
options: It eliminates the need for any quorum
It reduces the number of acceptors needed to just one
It uses Byzantine fault tolerance instead of crash tolerance
It allows proposers to contact acceptors directly, skipping the leader's propose step, at the cost of possible collisions
questions.explanation: Fast Paxos allows any proposer to send directly to acceptors, saving one message round-trip. However, concurrent proposals can collide and require a coordinator to resolve, sometimes making it slower than classic Paxos in practice.

questions.question: Which guarantees does Raft provide for its replicated log? (Select all that apply)
options: At most one leader per term
A leader's log is append-only and never has entries deleted
Committed entries will be present in the logs of all future leaders
Any node can overwrite the leader's log at any time
questions.explanation: Raft guarantees one leader per term, append-only leader logs, and that committed entries persist across leader changes. Followers never overwrite the leader's log; instead, the leader's log takes precedence.

title: Summary & Review
description: A final comparison of B+Trees and LSM Trees to review the major storage tradeoffs from the book.

questions.question: Which storage structure from the summary is generally the more write-optimized family?
options: B+Trees
LSM Trees
Static binary search trees
CRC trees
questions.explanation: The summary contrasts B+Trees as read-friendlier structures with LSM Trees as write-optimized structures that trade more read and compaction complexity for cheaper writes.

questions.question: Which properties describe a classic B+Tree in the summary's comparison framing? (Select all that apply)
options: Buffered
Mutable
Ordered
Append-only immutable on disk
questions.explanation: In the comparison table, B+Trees are presented as buffered, mutable, and ordered. Append-only immutable-on-disk behavior is more characteristic of LSM-style structures.

questions.question: Which page replacement algorithm tracks access frequency rather than recency?
options: FIFO
LRU
CLOCK
LFU
questions.explanation: LFU (Least Frequently Used) tracks how often each page is accessed and evicts the least frequently used one. LRU tracks recency, CLOCK approximates LRU, and FIFO simply uses insertion order.

questions.question: What is the fundamental insight that shapes storage engine design more than asymptotic complexity?
options: Hardware behavior, access patterns, and operational tradeoffs of the underlying storage medium
The choice of programming language
The number of users connected to the database
Whether the database is open-source or proprietary
questions.explanation: The summary emphasizes that real-world storage engine design is driven by hardware characteristics (HDD seek times, SSD page/block behavior), access patterns (sequential vs. random I/O), and operational tradeoffs (read vs. write vs. space amplification) rather than theoretical complexity alone.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 1 - Scale From Zero to Millions of Users
description: Horizontal scaling, caching, stateless web tiers, CDNs, etc.

questions.question: Why is a stateless web tier easier to scale horizontally?
options: Any web server can handle any request because session state is externalized
It removes the need for a database
It guarantees every request is served from a CDN
It makes vertical scaling unnecessary for all components
questions.explanation: When session state is stored outside the web server, load balancers can route each request to any healthy instance. This simplifies autoscaling, failover, and deployments.

questions.question: Which components commonly reduce load on origin servers in an early high-scale architecture? (Select all that apply)
options: Cache
Content delivery network
Load balancer
Single writable database primary
questions.explanation: Caches absorb repeated data reads, CDNs serve static assets near users, and load balancers distribute traffic across web instances. A single primary database can become a bottleneck instead of reducing origin load.

questions.question: What is the main tradeoff of database replication with a primary-replica setup?
options: It improves read scalability and failover, but replicas can lag behind the primary
It eliminates the need for backups
It makes every read strongly consistent by default
It prevents schema changes
questions.explanation: Read replicas improve read throughput and availability, but asynchronous replication introduces replica lag. Reads from replicas may be stale unless the design accounts for consistency requirements.

questions.question: When should a system usually introduce a message queue?
options: When work can be processed asynchronously to decouple producers from consumers
When every request must complete synchronously before returning
When static files need to be cached globally
When database indexes need to be dropped
questions.explanation: Queues smooth traffic spikes, isolate slow downstream work, and let workers retry background jobs independently of user-facing request latency.

questions.question: What is a common downside of caching data aggressively?
options: Cache invalidation and stale reads become harder to reason about
The database can no longer store persistent data
Every cache hit must be slower than a database hit
Load balancers stop working
questions.explanation: Caches improve latency and reduce database load, but introduce freshness and invalidation problems. Designs need TTLs, explicit invalidation, or write-through/write-around choices.

questions.question: Why are multiple data centers useful in large-scale systems?
options: They reduce disaster risk and can place traffic closer to users
They remove all consistency tradeoffs
They make every database write local to every user
They eliminate the need for monitoring
questions.explanation: Multi-data-center designs improve disaster recovery and geographic latency, but add replication, routing, failover, and consistency complexity.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 2 - Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
description: Statistics, conversions, and estimation strategies every software engineer should know.

questions.question: Why are powers of two useful in capacity estimation?
options: They map naturally to binary storage units such as KB, MB, GB, and TB
They guarantee exact user growth forecasts
They remove the need to estimate traffic
They make latency independent of network distance
questions.explanation: Storage and memory are commonly discussed in binary units, so powers of two help convert quickly between bytes, kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes, and terabytes.

questions.question: Which latency rule of thumb is most useful in system design interviews?
options: Memory access is fast, disk and network access are much slower
All storage media have roughly equal latency
Cross-region network calls are always faster than local memory reads
Sequential and random disk I/O have identical performance
questions.explanation: Knowing relative latency orders of magnitude helps decide when to cache, batch, avoid cross-region calls, or prefer sequential I/O.

questions.question: What does 99.9% availability roughly imply over a year?
options: About 8.8 hours of allowed downtime
About 8.8 seconds of allowed downtime
Zero downtime
One month of allowed downtime
questions.explanation: Three nines availability allows roughly 0.1% downtime per year, which is about 8.8 hours. More nines sharply reduce the error budget.

questions.question: Why should estimates usually separate QPS, storage, bandwidth, and cache size?
options: Each dimension stresses different parts of the system
They are always numerically identical
Only storage matters for distributed systems
Separating them prevents horizontal scaling
questions.explanation: QPS affects compute and databases, storage affects persistence, bandwidth affects networking/CDN cost, and cache size affects memory needs. Treating them separately exposes bottlenecks.

questions.question: What is the practical value of an SLA in design discussions?
options: It turns reliability expectations into an explicit availability or latency target
It replaces monitoring and alerting
It guarantees no failures can happen
It defines the exact database schema
questions.explanation: An SLA clarifies what the system must achieve and helps drive redundancy, fallback, monitoring, and error-budget decisions.

questions.question: Which approach is best when an estimate is uncertain in an interview?
options: State assumptions clearly and carry them through the calculation
Avoid estimating any number
Choose the largest possible value without explanation
Switch to implementation details immediately
questions.explanation: The interviewer is usually evaluating reasoning. Clear assumptions make the estimate debuggable and let the design adjust if a premise changes.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 3 - A Framework for System Design Interviews
description: A 4-step process for system design interviews, plus tips and tricks.

questions.question: What is the main goal of the first step in a system design interview?
options: Clarify requirements, constraints, users, and scope before designing
Draw the final architecture immediately
Choose a programming language
Write production-ready code
questions.explanation: Clarifying the problem prevents overbuilding the wrong system and establishes which functional and non-functional requirements matter most.

questions.question: Why should high-level design come before deep-dive details?
options: It gets alignment on the main components and data flows before optimizing internals
It avoids discussing tradeoffs
It proves the database schema is irrelevant
It guarantees the system is complete
questions.explanation: A shared high-level design gives the interviewer a chance to steer. The deep dive can then focus on the most important bottlenecks and tradeoffs.

questions.question: Which topics are usually worth clarifying early? (Select all that apply)
options: Functional requirements
Scale and traffic assumptions
Consistency and availability needs
CSS color palette
questions.explanation: Requirements, scale, and reliability constraints shape architecture. Visual styling is usually irrelevant unless the interview is specifically about frontend design.

questions.question: What is a good sign that a design deep dive is productive?
options: It focuses on the highest-risk bottleneck or ambiguity in the proposed design
It rewrites every component from scratch
It ignores the stated requirements
It spends all remaining time on unrelated technologies
questions.explanation: The deep dive should stress-test the parts most likely to fail at scale, such as data partitioning, hot keys, consistency, or retry behavior.

questions.question: Why is it useful to wrap up with bottlenecks and follow-ups?
options: It shows awareness of remaining risks and future improvements
It avoids discussing tradeoffs
It changes the requirements retroactively
It removes the need for monitoring
questions.explanation: A concise wrap-up demonstrates judgment: what the design handles, what it does not, and which tradeoffs would be revisited with more time.

questions.question: Which behavior is usually a design-interview anti-pattern?
options: Jumping into implementation details before validating requirements
Asking clarifying questions
Explaining tradeoffs
Estimating traffic
questions.explanation: Premature implementation details can solve the wrong problem. Good interviews usually begin with scope and requirements.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 4 - Design a Rate Limiter
description: High-level design breakdown and tradeoffs for distributed rate limiters.

questions.question: Why is client-side rate limiting insufficient as the main abuse-control mechanism?
options: Clients can bypass or modify client-side controls
It is always more expensive than server-side limiting
It cannot reduce polling frequency
It requires every client to use Redis
questions.explanation: Client-side throttling is helpful for cooperative clients, but adversarial clients can ignore it. Enforcement belongs on the server, API gateway, or load balancer path.

questions.question: What is the key behavior of a token bucket rate limiter?
options: Tokens refill over time and each accepted request consumes a token
Every request waits in a FIFO queue forever
Only requests in the previous fixed calendar minute are counted
The limiter stores a full log of every request body
questions.explanation: Token buckets support controlled average rate with burst allowance up to bucket capacity. They are common because they are simple and flexible.

questions.question: Which rate limiting algorithms can smooth bursts better than a plain fixed window? (Select all that apply)
options: Sliding window log
Sliding window counter
Token bucket
Naive fixed window only
questions.explanation: Sliding windows reduce boundary spikes, and token buckets regulate average rate while allowing bounded bursts. A naive fixed window can double-count bursts around window edges.

questions.question: Why is Redis often used for distributed rate limiting?
options: It provides fast shared counters with TTLs and atomic operations
It guarantees unlimited memory
It replaces all API servers
It makes user identification unnecessary
questions.explanation: A distributed limiter needs shared state across servers. Redis supports low-latency increments, expirations, and Lua scripts for atomic multi-step checks.

questions.question: What is the fail-open vs fail-closed tradeoff in a rate limiter?
options: Fail-open preserves availability but may allow abuse; fail-closed protects capacity but may block valid users
Fail-open disables all logging; fail-closed enables all logging
Fail-open is always strongly consistent; fail-closed is eventually consistent
They only differ in response body formatting
questions.explanation: If the limiter dependency fails, a product must choose whether to allow traffic through or reject it. The right choice depends on risk, revenue, and abuse tolerance.

questions.question: How can hot keys affect a distributed rate limiter?
options: A single popular client or endpoint can overload one shard of limiter state
They make all requests anonymous
They eliminate the need for counters
They only affect static assets
questions.explanation: If a heavily used key maps to one Redis shard or process, that shard can bottleneck. Mitigations include key splitting, local pre-aggregation, and careful sharding.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 5 - Consistent Hashing
description: Consistent hashing strategies for servers and database shards.

questions.question: What problem does consistent hashing solve compared with hash(key) % N?
options: It reduces the amount of key movement when nodes are added or removed
It removes the need for replication
It guarantees perfect balance for all workloads
It prevents hot keys from existing
questions.explanation: Modulo hashing remaps many keys whenever N changes. Consistent hashing confines most movement to neighboring ranges on the ring.

questions.question: What are virtual nodes used for in a consistent hash ring?
options: Improving load balance by giving each physical node multiple positions on the ring
Encrypting object keys
Replacing replicas with caches
Forcing all traffic to one primary node
questions.explanation: Virtual nodes spread each physical server across the ring, which smooths uneven hash-space ownership and simplifies capacity weighting.

questions.question: How can a consistent hash ring support heterogeneous servers?
options: Assign stronger servers more virtual nodes
Disable replication on stronger servers
Hash only small objects
Use a fixed window counter
questions.explanation: Weighted virtual nodes let larger servers own more ranges while smaller servers own fewer. This is a practical way to reflect different capacities.

questions.question: What remains a problem even with consistent hashing?
options: Hot keys can still overload the nodes responsible for them
Keys can no longer be found
Adding nodes becomes impossible
Replication is mathematically forbidden
questions.explanation: Consistent hashing balances key ranges, not access frequency. A single extremely popular key still needs mitigation such as replication, caching, or request coalescing.

questions.question: Which operations are most directly affected by node joins and leaves in consistent hashing? (Select all that apply)
options: Range ownership transfer
