Replica placement
Cache warmup
HTML rendering in clients
questions.explanation: Membership changes move ownership for affected ranges, alter replica sets, and can create cold caches. Client-side rendering is unrelated.

questions.question: Why is a hash ring often paired with replication?
options: So data remains available when the owner node fails
So all writes become single-threaded
So keys become human-readable
So the ring no longer needs membership tracking
questions.explanation: Replication stores copies on additional nodes, improving availability and durability when a node or range owner fails.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 6 - Design a Key-Value Store
description: Considerations when designing a highly available distributed key-value store.

questions.question: In a distributed key-value store, what does quorum tuning control?
options: The number of replicas that must acknowledge reads and writes
The number of keys in a JSON object
The number of CPU cores on each client
The visual layout of monitoring dashboards
questions.explanation: Quorum parameters such as N, R, and W trade latency and availability against consistency. Higher R or W usually improves consistency but costs more latency and failure sensitivity.

questions.question: What does the condition R + W > N usually provide in quorum systems?
options: Read and write quorums overlap, increasing the chance of reading the latest write
All replicas are guaranteed Byzantine fault tolerant
Writes never need to be replicated
Reads can ignore every replica
questions.explanation: If read and write quorums overlap, at least one read replica should have seen the latest successful write in a healthy quorum-based system.

questions.question: Why are vector clocks useful in eventually consistent key-value stores?
options: They help detect concurrent conflicting versions that cannot be ordered causally
They synchronize physical clocks across data centers
They compress values before storage
They replace all replication protocols
questions.explanation: Vector clocks track version causality across replicas. If neither version descends from the other, the system can expose a conflict for resolution.

questions.question: What is hinted handoff designed to handle?
options: Temporary replica unavailability by storing a write on another node until the target recovers
Permanent deletion of all replicas
Schema migrations in relational databases
Client-side image compression
questions.explanation: When a target replica is unavailable, another node can temporarily accept the write with a hint and deliver it later. This improves availability but may weaken immediate consistency.

questions.question: How do Merkle trees help anti-entropy repair?
options: They compare hashes of key ranges so replicas can find divergent data efficiently
They route HTTP requests to API gateways
They assign globally unique IDs
They enforce rate limits
questions.explanation: Merkle trees summarize ranges with hashes. Replicas compare tree branches and only exchange the ranges that differ, avoiding full dataset scans.

questions.question: Which mechanisms are commonly part of Dynamo-style key-value stores? (Select all that apply)
options: Consistent hashing
Quorum reads/writes
Gossip membership
Single-node-only storage
questions.explanation: Dynamo-style systems combine partitioning via consistent hashing, tunable quorum operations, and gossip-based cluster membership/failure detection.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 7 - Design a Unique ID Generator
description: Various approaches to distributed ID generation, including UUID, Ticket Server, Snowflake IDs, etc.

questions.question: Why are auto-increment IDs difficult in multi-master systems?
options: Independent writers can generate the same number without coordination
They cannot be stored in databases
They are always longer than UUIDs
They prevent indexing
questions.explanation: If several masters allocate IDs independently, they need coordination or partitioned ID ranges to avoid collisions.

questions.question: What is a major advantage of UUIDs for distributed ID generation?
options: They can be generated independently with extremely low collision probability
They are always time-sortable
They are shorter than 64-bit integers
They encode the shard location by default
questions.explanation: UUIDs avoid a central coordinator and work across machines and regions, but their size and poor locality can be downsides.

questions.question: What is the core weakness of a ticket server for ID generation?
options: It can become a single point of failure and throughput bottleneck
It cannot issue numeric IDs
It makes IDs globally unique without coordination
It prevents batching
questions.explanation: A central ticket server is simple and can issue sequential IDs, but it must be highly available and scalable or the whole system's writes are affected.

questions.question: What fields are typically combined in a Snowflake-style ID?
options: Timestamp, machine or data-center identifier, and sequence number
User password, URL path, and cache TTL
Primary key, foreign key, and SQL query plan
Image size, MIME type, and CDN region
questions.explanation: Snowflake IDs usually pack time, worker identity, and an incrementing sequence into a sortable fixed-width integer.

questions.question: Why must Snowflake-style systems handle clock rollback carefully?
options: A backward clock can cause duplicate or non-monotonic IDs on the same worker
It makes all IDs shorter
It disables network routing
It turns integer IDs into UUIDs
questions.explanation: If a worker's timestamp moves backward, it may reuse a previous timestamp and sequence range. Systems usually wait, reject, or use logical safeguards.

questions.question: Which ID generation approaches avoid a central service on the write path? (Select all that apply)
options: UUIDs
Snowflake-style workers
A single ticket server
Database auto-increment on one primary
questions.explanation: UUIDs and Snowflake-style workers can generate IDs locally. Ticket servers and single-primary auto-increment schemes centralize ID allocation.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 8 - Design a URL Shortener
description: Designing a URL shortener like bit.ly or TinyURL.

questions.question: Why is Base62 commonly used for short URLs?
options: It compactly encodes IDs using digits, uppercase letters, and lowercase letters
It encrypts URLs end to end
It prevents all hash collisions
It requires only decimal digits
questions.explanation: Base62 provides a URL-friendly alphabet with 62 characters, letting large numeric IDs be represented in short strings.

questions.question: What is the main issue with hash-based short URL generation?
options: Different long URLs can collide on the same shortened hash prefix
It cannot produce fixed-length strings
It requires a global counter
It makes redirects impossible
questions.explanation: Hash prefixes are compact but can collide. Collision handling usually checks the database and retries with a longer hash or salt.

questions.question: What is a practical advantage of counter + Base62 over hashing?
options: It naturally creates unique short codes if the counter is unique
It hides all business volume by default
It requires no database lookup on redirect
It guarantees no one can enumerate links
questions.explanation: A unique counter maps cleanly to a unique Base62 code. The tradeoff is that sequential codes can expose volume and are easier to enumerate unless mitigated.

questions.question: When is a 301 redirect usually preferable for a short URL?
options: When the mapping is permanent and client/browser caching is acceptable
When every click must be counted at the origin
When the long URL changes every second
When caching must be disabled
questions.explanation: A 301 is permanent and can be cached by clients, reducing load. A 302 is better when analytics or mutable mappings require requests to keep reaching the service.

questions.question: Which data is typically stored for a shortened URL? (Select all that apply)
options: Short code
Original long URL
Creation or expiration metadata
Every user's password
questions.explanation: The service needs the code-to-URL mapping and operational metadata such as owner, creation time, expiration, and analytics counters. User passwords are unrelated and should not be stored in mapping rows.

questions.question: Why is caching valuable in URL redirecting?
options: Popular short codes can be resolved without hitting the primary database
It makes all redirects strongly consistent
It removes the need to store the original URL
It prevents HTTP redirects from being cached by browsers
questions.explanation: Redirect traffic is read-heavy and skewed. Caching hot mappings cuts database load and lowers redirect latency.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 9 - Design a Web Crawler
description: Designing a Web Crawler for text extraction and LLM training data.

questions.question: Why do many crawlers use breadth-first search as a baseline?
options: It explores pages by link distance from seeds and avoids going too deep into one site
It guarantees every page has equal priority
It eliminates duplicate URLs
It makes robots.txt unnecessary
questions.explanation: BFS is a reasonable starting point for broad coverage, though production crawlers add priority, politeness, freshness, and deduplication controls.

questions.question: What does crawler politeness protect against?
options: Overloading a target website with too many requests too quickly
Hash collisions in short URLs
Duplicate Snowflake IDs
Slow image transcoding
questions.explanation: Politeness enforces per-host delays and robots.txt rules so the crawler does not harm the sites it visits.

questions.question: What is the URL frontier responsible for?
options: Managing which URLs should be crawled next and when
Storing user sessions
Issuing TLS certificates
Rendering frontend pages
questions.explanation: The frontier is the scheduler for crawl work. It balances priority, politeness, freshness, and distributed worker assignment.

questions.question: Which crawler mechanisms improve efficiency? (Select all that apply)
options: URL deduplication
Content fingerprinting
Per-host scheduling
Retrying every failed URL forever without backoff
questions.explanation: Deduplication avoids repeated work, fingerprints detect duplicate content, and per-host scheduling improves politeness. Infinite retries can waste capacity.

questions.question: Why does freshness matter in web crawling?
options: Pages change over time, so important pages should be revisited on an appropriate schedule
It ensures every URL is crawled exactly once
It removes the need for parsers
It prevents DNS failures
questions.explanation: A crawler needs recrawl policies so stale index data is updated without wasting resources on pages that rarely change.

questions.question: How can a crawler be made extensible?
options: Use modular fetchers, parsers, extractors, and storage pipelines
Hard-code all logic into a single worker
Disable content-type detection
Avoid queues
questions.explanation: A modular pipeline makes it easier to add new content types, parsers, ranking signals, and storage sinks without rewriting the whole crawler.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 10 - Design a Notification System
description: Designing a notification system that supports push notifications, SMS, and email.

questions.question: Why do notification systems usually integrate with third-party providers?
options: Mobile push, SMS, and email delivery depend on external platforms and carriers
They cannot store templates locally
They must use a single database table for every channel
They avoid all delivery failures
questions.explanation: APNs/FCM, email providers, and SMS gateways are specialized delivery channels. The system must abstract over their APIs, quotas, errors, and retries.

questions.question: What is the purpose of notification templates?
options: Provide reusable, localized, and consistently formatted message bodies
Replace user preferences
Guarantee delivery through SMS carriers
Shard the user table
questions.explanation: Templates keep notification content consistent, easier to localize, and safer to update without changing core delivery code.

questions.question: Which features help prevent notification spam? (Select all that apply)
options: User preferences
Rate limiting
Deduplication or batching
Unlimited retries with no backoff
questions.explanation: Preferences, rate limits, deduplication, and batching reduce unwanted or excessive notifications. Unbounded retries can amplify spam and provider load.

questions.question: Why is a queue useful between notification creation and provider delivery?
options: It decouples producers from provider latency and supports retry workers
It proves delivery succeeded
It removes the need for provider credentials
It makes every notification synchronous
questions.explanation: Queues absorb bursts, isolate slow providers, and let workers retry or route messages without blocking user-facing requests.

questions.question: What should monitoring track in a notification system?
options: Delivery success rates, provider errors, queue lag, and latency
Only database CPU
Only template character count
Only frontend paint time
questions.explanation: Delivery systems need visibility into queue backlog, channel-specific success/failure rates, provider throttling, and end-to-end latency.

questions.question: Why is guaranteed notification delivery hard?
options: External providers and devices can fail, throttle, or be offline
Templates cannot be cached
Users cannot have multiple devices
Every provider has identical semantics
questions.explanation: The system can guarantee durable enqueueing and retries, but final delivery depends on provider behavior, device state, user settings, and channel semantics.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 11 - Design a News Feed
description: Designing a news feed system like the Facebook or Twitter timeline.

questions.question: What is fanout on write in a news feed system?
options: Precomputing and pushing a new post into followers' feed inboxes when it is published
Computing every user's feed only when they open the app
Sending notifications through SMS only
Hashing URLs into short codes
questions.explanation: Fanout on write shifts work to publish time, making reads fast for ordinary users but expensive for authors with many followers.

questions.question: What is fanout on read?
options: Building the feed at read time by pulling recent posts from followed users
Writing every post to all follower inboxes
Storing only image thumbnails
Sending every feed item through a rate limiter
questions.explanation: Fanout on read avoids massive write amplification for high-follower accounts, but read latency and query complexity increase.

questions.question: Why do many feed systems use a hybrid fanout strategy?
options: Normal users use fanout on write, while celebrities or high-fanout users are pulled at read time
All users are always handled by one SQL query
It removes the need for caching
It guarantees chronological ordering only
questions.explanation: Hybrid fanout keeps reads fast for most relationships while avoiding huge publish-time work for accounts with very large follower sets.

questions.question: Which stores are commonly involved in a feed design? (Select all that apply)
options: Post/object store
User graph or follower store
Feed cache/inbox store
DNS zone file as the primary database
questions.explanation: Feeds need post content, social graph data, and low-latency feed materialization/caching. DNS is not a primary feed data store.

questions.question: Why is caching important for feed retrieval?
options: Feed reads are frequent and latency-sensitive
It removes the need to store posts durably
It prevents users from following others
It makes all ranking algorithms unnecessary
questions.explanation: Users read feeds far more often than they publish. Caching feed IDs, post objects, and user profiles reduces latency and backend load.

questions.question: What problem does a celebrity user create for fanout on write?
options: A single post may require writes to millions of follower feeds
The user cannot publish text posts
The user bypasses all databases
The user's feed must be deleted
questions.explanation: Very high follower counts cause write amplification and queue spikes. Systems often treat these users specially with pull-time merge or delayed fanout.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 12 - Design a Chat System
description: Designing a chat system like Slack or WhatsApp.

questions.question: Why are persistent connections important for chat systems?
options: They allow servers to push new messages to online clients in near real time
They remove the need for message storage
They guarantee every message is read
They make all clients stateless
questions.explanation: WebSocket-like persistent connections let the server deliver messages without client polling, improving latency and efficiency.

questions.question: What does a chat service need service discovery for?
options: Finding which chat server owns or currently holds a user's connection
Converting text into video
Generating Base62 URLs
Computing CDN cache TTLs
questions.explanation: In a distributed chat system, routing services need to know where a user's active connection lives so messages can be delivered to the right server.

questions.question: Why is layer 4 load balancing often relevant for chat connections?
options: It can distribute long-lived TCP connections without terminating application protocols
It stores chat history
It guarantees message ordering across all conversations
It replaces mobile push notifications
questions.explanation: Chat uses long-lived connections. L4 load balancers can distribute connections efficiently while chat servers manage protocol-level state.

questions.question: What storage pattern is useful for one-to-one chat history?
options: Partition messages by conversation or participant pair and order by message time/ID
Store every message only in browser memory
Use a CDN as the primary message database
Store messages under random keys with no ordering
questions.explanation: Conversation-based partitioning and ordered message IDs make recent history retrieval efficient and preserve message order within a chat.

questions.question: Which mechanisms support offline users in chat? (Select all that apply)
options: Durable message storage
Push notifications
Unread state
Dropping all messages sent while offline
questions.explanation: Offline delivery requires messages to be stored, unread state to be tracked, and push notifications to wake devices when appropriate.

questions.question: Why are presence indicators challenging at scale?
options: Online/offline status changes frequently and must be fanned out to interested users
They require video transcoding
They cannot use heartbeats
They are always strongly consistent globally
questions.explanation: Presence depends on heartbeats and connection state. Frequent updates must be aggregated and selectively distributed to avoid overwhelming the system.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 13 - Design a Search Autocomplete System
description: Designing a search autocomplete system like the Google search bar.

questions.question: Why is a trie useful for autocomplete?
options: It organizes strings by prefix, making prefix lookup efficient
It stores videos in multiple bitrates
It guarantees eventual consistency
It encrypts search terms
questions.explanation: A trie lets the service traverse characters in the prefix and then retrieve candidate completions from that prefix node.

questions.question: What is usually stored at trie nodes to serve autocomplete quickly?
options: Top-k suggestions or references for that prefix
Full user session cookies
Every video transcoding job
Rate-limit headers
questions.explanation: Precomputing top-k suggestions at each prefix node makes serving requests fast, at the cost of update and storage complexity.

questions.question: Why are autocomplete frequency updates often batched?
options: Immediate trie updates for every query can be too expensive and noisy
Batches make suggestions impossible to cache
Users only type in batches
Batching prevents ranking changes forever
questions.explanation: Aggregating search frequencies in logs or streams and updating periodically reduces write load and smooths short-lived noise.

questions.question: Which factors can influence autocomplete ranking? (Select all that apply)
options: Query frequency
Freshness or trending signals
User locale/language
Disk block checksum only
questions.explanation: Popularity, recency, personalization, and locale often affect ranking. Storage checksums are not ranking signals.

questions.question: Why is caching especially effective for autocomplete?
options: Many users request the same short prefixes repeatedly
Every query is globally unique
It removes the need to rank suggestions
It guarantees no stale suggestions
questions.explanation: Short prefixes such as one or two characters are extremely hot. Caching prefix results can absorb substantial read traffic.

questions.question: What is a tradeoff of storing top-k suggestions at every trie node?
options: Low read latency but higher storage and update cost
No storage overhead but slow reads
Perfect personalization with no complexity
No need for ranking data
questions.explanation: Materialized top-k lists make serving fast, but every ranking update may affect many prefix nodes and consume more memory/storage.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 14 - Design a Video Sharing Platform
description: Designing a video sharing platform like YouTube.

questions.question: Why do video platforms transcode uploaded videos?
options: To produce formats, resolutions, and bitrates suitable for different devices and networks
To make every file smaller than one byte
To avoid storing metadata
To replace CDNs
questions.explanation: Transcoding creates multiple playable representations so clients can stream smoothly across devices, browsers, and network conditions.

questions.question: What is adaptive bitrate streaming designed to do?
options: Switch video quality based on available bandwidth and playback conditions
Force every user to watch the highest bitrate
Disable buffering entirely
Store videos only in a relational database
questions.explanation: Adaptive streaming lets clients choose among encoded segments at different bitrates, improving playback stability under changing network conditions.

questions.question: Why are pre-signed URLs useful for large video uploads?
options: Clients can upload directly to object storage without proxying bytes through application servers
They remove all authentication
They transcode video in the browser
They guarantee every upload completes
questions.explanation: Direct-to-object-storage uploads reduce app server bandwidth and make large upload paths more scalable while preserving scoped authorization.

questions.question: What makes resumable uploads important for video systems?
options: Large uploads are likely to be interrupted and should resume from uploaded chunks
Small files cannot use HTTP
They prevent the need for object storage
They make encoding unnecessary
questions.explanation: Videos can be large, so chunked/resumable uploads avoid restarting from zero after transient network or client failures.

questions.question: Which components are commonly in a video processing pipeline? (Select all that apply)
options: Upload storage
Encoding/transcoding workers
Metadata database
Autocomplete trie
questions.explanation: Video systems store originals, run asynchronous processing workers, and track metadata/status. Autocomplete tries are unrelated.

questions.question: Why do video streaming systems rely heavily on CDNs?
options: Video traffic is bandwidth-heavy and benefits from edge caching near viewers
CDNs are required to generate unique IDs
CDNs replace all upload processing
CDNs guarantee every video is popular
questions.explanation: Serving video from edge locations reduces origin load, bandwidth cost, and playback latency for geographically distributed users.

title: Vol. 1 Ch. 15 - Design Google Drive
description: Designing a file storage service like Google Drive or Dropbox.

questions.question: Why do cloud storage systems split large files into blocks?
options: Blocks support resumable uploads, deduplication, checksums, and partial retries
Blocks remove the need for metadata
Blocks make all files exactly the same size
Blocks prevent clients from downloading files
questions.explanation: Block-level storage lets the system retry only failed chunks, verify integrity, sync changed portions, and potentially deduplicate repeated content.

questions.question: What does the metadata database track in a Google Drive-like system?
options: File ownership, versions, block references, sync state, and permissions metadata
Raw bytes for every file block only
Video transcoding bitrates only
Global rate limit headers only
questions.explanation: Object/block storage holds file bytes, while metadata stores the logical file model, versions, ownership, paths, and references to blocks.

questions.question: Why are checksums important in a file sync service?
options: They verify block integrity and detect corrupted or mismatched data
They replace authentication
They make conflicts impossible
They choose the nearest data center
questions.explanation: Checksums allow clients and servers to confirm that uploaded/downloaded blocks match expected content and to identify changed blocks.

questions.question: What causes sync conflicts in cloud file storage?
options: Multiple devices edit the same file while not seeing each other's latest version
A file is downloaded once
A CDN caches a static image
A user logs in from one device only
questions.explanation: Availability-oriented sync allows offline or concurrent edits. If versions diverge, the system must detect conflicts and preserve user data.

questions.question: Which features help support large file uploads? (Select all that apply)
options: Chunking
Resumable upload sessions
Parallel block upload
Single request with no retry state
questions.explanation: Chunking and resumable sessions let large uploads recover from failures, and parallel block upload can improve throughput. A single untracked request is fragile.

questions.question: What is a cost-saving technique for old or rarely accessed files?
options: Move cold data to cheaper storage tiers
Store every file only in memory
Disable checksums
Keep all replicas in the most expensive region
questions.explanation: Lifecycle policies can move cold blocks to lower-cost storage while keeping metadata and hot data readily accessible.
